intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with or without macrocephaly (NEDMAC) is caused by hemizygous or heterozygous mutation in the SMARCA1 gene on chromosome X.

checks.evidence_quote: An additional 25 families were ascertained in part through the MatchMaker Exchange network for a total of 35 individuals with apparent non-mosaic hemizygous or heterozygous SMARCA1 variants.

checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic SNF2 related chromatin remodeling ATPase 1 (SMARCA1) variants have been reported in patients with X-linked intellectual disability (XLID)

paragraphs.text: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without macrocephaly (NEDMAC) is an X-linked disorder with a broad clinical spectrum. Its most frequent features are mild to severe intellectual disability or developmental delay and delayed or regressive speech development. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) features, other behavioral difficulties, facial dysmorphism, and other variable features also occur, and macrocephaly is present in about half of patients. Most affected individuals are hemizygous males. Heterozygous females are also affected and often have a milder phenotype (Mirzaa et al., 2025).

checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic variants in SMARCA1 cause an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder modulated by NURF complex composition.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) reported 35 individuals (26 males and 9 females) from 26 families. Ages at last clinical assessment ranged from 2 to 49 years. The index family spanned 6 generations and included 4 individuals with mild to severe intellectual disability or developmental delay and brain overgrowth. Across the cohort, the most common features were intellectual disability or developmental delay (77%; 27/35) and speech delay and/or speech regression (83%; 29/35); in 4 individuals speech regression was noted rather than delay. Seventeen of 35 individuals (49%) had increased head circumference (OFC at least +2 SD) and/or reported macrocephaly or brain overgrowth. Increased height (at least +2 SD) was reported in 29%. Other features included: - motor delay (20/34) - seizures or epilepsy (8/35) - hypotonia (15/35) - behavioral difficulties such as ASD, ADHD, or aggression (19/35); in some instances (9/25) these were linked to regression in speech and mental development - an ASD diagnosis (11/35) Dysmorphic facial features were reported in 19 of 35 individuals. Photographs of 7 patients showed frontal bossing, a long face, slanted palpebral fissures, a flat nasal root with a short bulbous nose, anteverted nares, and a thin upper lip. In the index family, the proband had an OFC of +6 SD, severe intellectual disability, no language, ASD, hydrocephalus treated with a shunt, hepatosplenomegaly, and height and weight of +5 SD. The 2 heterozygous carrier mothers in this family, aged 45 and 49 years, had OFCs of +1 SD and +1.5 SD and no reported learning disability.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) performed genome-wide DNA methylation analysis on peripheral blood DNA from 19 individuals with SMARCA1 variants. Compared with 57 matched controls, the samples showed a predominantly hypomethylated profile defined by 232 probes. Separate profiles were also found for males and for females. The authors concluded that this mild global methylation profile, shared by patients with truncating variants and overgrowth, was not robust enough to be considered an epi-signature.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of NEDMAC is X-linked, according to Mirzaa et al. (2025). Among the 26 index cases they reported, 17 had a maternally inherited variant and 4 had de novo variants. Segregation was not determined in the remaining 5, 4 of whom were presumed to have maternally inherited variants. Affected individuals included both hemizygous males and heterozygous females. Nishimura et al. (2025) found that the variants in their 2 affected males were inherited from unaffected healthy mothers.

paragraphs.text: Nishimura et al. (2025) used exome sequencing to identify hemizygous SMARCA1 variants in 2 unrelated males with X-linked intellectual disability. Patient 1 had a nonsense variant (Q599X) leading to nonsense-mediated decay. Patient 2 had a missense variant (R448L), which structural modeling suggested might destabilize interactions between SMARCA1 and nucleosomal DNA. Both variants were inherited from unaffected mothers.

paragraphs.text: In a 6-generation family with 4 affected individuals, Mirzaa et al. (2025) used exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous nonsense mutation in the SMARCA1 gene (R91X). Further families were ascertained in part through the MatchMaker Exchange network, giving a total of 35 individuals from 26 families with apparent non-mosaic hemizygous or heterozygous SMARCA1 variants. Variants were identified by trio-based exome sequencing in 23 families and by whole-genome sequencing in 3 families. There were 25 unique variants, and a second unrelated family carried the same variant as the index family. The variants comprised 7 nonsense variants, 3 frameshift indels, and 15 missense variants. All were predicted to be deleterious by multiple algorithms. Sixteen of the 25 lay within the ATPase domain (12) or the HSS domain (4). In transfected U2OS cells, 4 patient variants (R253X, R259G, R751Q, and E771K) each produced a stable protein that localized to the nucleus. The authors also identified SMARCA1 variants in 7 additional families that they considered likely non-causative or not explanatory. These included V384M, found in 3 families; it had previously been reported in a family with schizophrenia and is present in gnomAD, including in 7 hemizygotes.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found macrocephaly in 70% of individuals with truncating variants. However, 3 individuals with truncating variants did not have brain overgrowth, and 4 individuals with missense variants did. The authors therefore concluded that macrocephaly is not restricted to individuals with putative loss-of-function variants. Individuals in the DECIPHER database with CNV deletions encompassing SMARCA1 did not have macrocephaly. Of the 9 affected females, 7 had truncating variants; 3 of these had macrocephaly and 4 did not. Macrocephaly was discordant in 2 mother-daughter pairs. The authors proposed that variants associated with macrocephaly act in a dominant-negative fashion and that variants without macrocephaly act as functional hypomorphs.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found that Smarca1 knockout mice were viable with no obvious gross developmental defects. Their brains showed only slight size reductions and no deficits in cortical progenitors or lamination. In behavioral testing, the knockout mice were more active than wildtype mice in the dark but otherwise showed no significant differences. In contrast, Smarca1ex6del mice, which make an internally truncated protein, had a total brain area 10% larger than controls. This enlargement was reduced when Smarca5 was also ablated. In Smarca1 knockout cerebellum, SMARCA5 co-immunoprecipitated with CECR2, suggesting that SMARCA5 compensated for the loss of SMARCA1.

agent.process_note: I read Mirzaa et al. (2025) in full through the Methods section, including Table 1 and the mouse, methylation and functional results. I read the abstracts of Nishimura et al. (2025) and Lopes et al. (2016), which are the only text available for those papers. For Karaca et al. (2015) and Riazuddin et al. (2017), I searched for SMARCA1, hemizygous/X-linked and the family IDs (BAB4453, PKMR142) and read those passages. Riazuddin gives only a table entry for a Punjabi family's missense variant, with no zygosity or segregation stated. Karaca's text calls the variant hemizygous but its figure legend calls it homozygous; I used hemizygous. Lopes's abstract does not give the SMARCA1 variant or the patient's sex. No reference data were supplied for SMARCA1's MIM number or cytogenetic location, so the intro says only 'chromosome X'.
